detailedAnswer: JDK contains JRE, JRE contains JVM. Source compiles to bytecode with javac; the JVM loads, verifies, and executes bytecode, with JIT compilation for hot code. Portability comes from bytecode plus a platform-specific JVM. Remember: JDK is for development (compiler, tools), JRE is for running (libraries + JVM), JVM is the runtime engine itself. Class loading, bytecode verification, and the runtime memory areas (heap, stack, metaspace) are the usual follow-up topics.
question: Module 0 revision: JDK, JRE, JVM in one minute
shortAnswer: JDK ⊃ JRE ⊃ JVM; source → bytecode → JVM execution → JIT for hot code.
tips: If asked 'is Java fully platform independent?', answer: bytecode is portable, but the JVM itself is platform-specific.
title: Revision: JVM basics

detailedAnswer: Encapsulation: bundle data with the methods that use it and expose it only through controlled access (private fields, public methods). Abstraction: expose what an object does, not how (abstract classes and interfaces). Inheritance: a subclass reuses and extends a superclass — favour composition over inheritance when reuse is not truly an is-a relationship. Polymorphism: the same call behaves differently by runtime type — method overriding (runtime) versus overloading (compile time). In an interview, always give a concrete example: e.g. a Payment interface with CardPayment and UpiPayment implementations, chosen at runtime.
question: Module 0 revision: OOP in one minute
shortAnswer: Encapsulation hides state, abstraction hides complexity, inheritance reuses behaviour, polymorphism lets one interface take many forms.
tips: Name all four pillars, then immediately give one real example — interviewers remember examples, not definitions alone.
title: Revision: OOP principles

commonMistakes: Comparing strings with == instead of equals().
Concatenating inside a loop instead of using StringBuilder.
detailedAnswer: String is immutable: every concatenation creates a new object, so building strings in a loop with + is slow — use StringBuilder (single-threaded) or StringBuffer (synchronized). Literals are interned in the string pool, so "abc" == "abc" can be true, but never rely on it: compare content with equals(), and use equalsIgnoreCase() or Objects.equals() when nulls are possible. String is final, so it cannot be subclassed, which also makes it safe as a HashMap key. Know the common traps: String.split takes a regex, substring and trim return new strings, and string comparison with == is the classic interview bug.
question: Module 0 revision: Strings in one minute
shortAnswer: String is immutable and pooled; use StringBuilder for loops, equals() for content, == only for reference identity.
title: Revision: Strings

detailedAnswer: List allows duplicates and is ordered; Set forbids duplicates; Map stores key-value pairs with unique keys. ArrayList gives fast random access; LinkedList is better for frequent inserts/removes in the middle but slow for random access. HashMap gives fast key lookup but no ordering guarantee — use LinkedHashMap for insertion order, TreeMap for sorted keys. HashSet is backed by a HashMap; TreeSet keeps elements sorted. ConcurrentHashMap is the thread-safe map choice, with no null keys or values, unlike HashMap (one null key, many null values) and Hashtable (synchronized, no nulls). Always state time complexity: ArrayList get is O(1), HashMap get/put is O(1) on average.
question: Module 0 revision: Collections in one minute
shortAnswer: List: ordered + duplicates. Set: unique. Map: key-value. ArrayList for access, HashMap for lookup, ConcurrentHashMap for shared maps.
tips: When asked 'which collection?', answer with the access pattern first: ordered? unique? keyed? thread-safe? — then name the class.
title: Revision: Collections

commonMistakes: Catching Exception before its subclasses, which does not compile.
Using exceptions for normal control flow.
detailedAnswer: Throwable splits into Error (serious JVM problems, do not catch) and Exception. Checked exceptions (e.g. IOException) must be caught or declared with throws; unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and subclasses, e.g. NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException) need not be declared. Use try-with-resources for anything AutoCloseable so resources close even on failure. Catch the most specific exception first — a broad catch of Exception hides bugs. Never swallow an exception with an empty catch block: log it or rethrow it, possibly wrapped. In Spring apps, prefer translating checked exceptions into meaningful runtime exceptions at service boundaries and handling them centrally with @ControllerAdvice.
question: Module 0 revision: Exceptions in one minute
shortAnswer: Checked exceptions must be handled or declared; unchecked (RuntimeException) need not be. Catch specific exceptions, use try-with-resources, never swallow exceptions.
title: Revision: Exceptions

detailedAnswer: Generics let you write one class or method that works for many types while the compiler checks types for you — List<String> cannot accidentally hold an Integer. Because of type erasure, generic type information is removed at compile time: you cannot do new T(), check instanceof List<String>, or overload foo(List<String>) and foo(List<Integer>) together. Wildcards: <? extends T> is a producer (you read from it, PECS), <? super T> is a consumer (you write into it). Bounded type parameters (<T extends Comparable<T>>) restrict what a type argument may be. Generics do not work with primitives — use wrapper classes and autoboxing, and be aware of the small boxing cost in hot loops.
question: Module 0 revision: Generics in one minute
shortAnswer: Generics give compile-time type safety; type erasure means generic types do not exist at runtime. PECS: producer extends, consumer super.
tips: PECS is the single most-asked generics point: say it, then give an example (copying from List<? extends Number> into List<? super Number>).
title: Revision: Generics

commonMistakes: Reusing a stream after a terminal operation.
Using forEach to mutate shared state inside a parallel stream.
detailedAnswer: A stream pipeline has a source (collection, array, generator), zero or more intermediate operations (filter, map, flatMap, sorted, distinct — lazy, return a stream), and exactly one terminal operation (collect, forEach, reduce, count, anyMatch — triggers execution). Streams do not modify the source and are single-use: reuse throws IllegalStateException. Intermediate operations are lazy, so filter().map() does nothing until a terminal operation runs, which enables short-circuiting with findFirst() or limit(). A lambda is shorthand for an anonymous implementation of a functional interface (one abstract method), e.g. (a, b) -> a + b for a Comparator. Method references (String::toUpperCase, System.out::println) are lambdas in shorter form. Parallel streams split work across threads, but only help for large, CPU-bound, stateless pipelines — never use them with shared mutable state.
question: Module 0 revision: Streams in one minute
shortAnswer: Streams are lazy pipelines: source → intermediate operations → one terminal operation. Lambdas are concise implementations of functional interfaces.
title: Revision: Streams and lambdas

detailedAnswer: Optional is a container that is either empty or holds one non-null value: use Optional.ofNullable(value), map/flatMap to transform, orElse/orElseGet for a fallback, and orElseThrow for a meaningful exception. Prefer orElseGet over orElse when the fallback is expensive, because orElse evaluates eagerly. Never call get() without checking, never use Optional as a method parameter or a field in an entity, and never return null where you promised an Optional. The built-in functional interfaces: Predicate<T> (test, returns boolean), Function<T,R> (apply), Consumer<T> (accept, no result), Supplier<T> (get, no input), plus BiFunction, BiPredicate, and primitive versions like IntPredicate and ToIntFunction that avoid boxing. Custom functional interfaces need exactly one abstract method and are usually marked @FunctionalInterface.
question: Module 0 revision: Optional and functional interfaces in one minute
shortAnswer: Optional models 'value may be absent' explicitly. Core functional interfaces: Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier, plus Bi- variants and primitive specializations.
tips: If asked why not just return null: Optional forces the caller to handle absence at compile time instead of discovering a NullPointerException at runtime.
title: Revision: Optional and functional interfaces

commonMistakes: Creating unbounded threads instead of using a pool.
Assuming volatile makes compound actions atomic.
Forgetting to shut down an ExecutorService.
detailedAnswer: Each thread has its own stack; all threads share the heap, which is why unsynchronized access to shared mutable state causes race conditions. synchronized and ReentrantLock provide mutual exclusion; volatile guarantees visibility of a variable's latest value but not atomicity (volatile++ is still a race). Prefer the java.util.concurrent toolkit: ExecutorService and thread pools instead of new Thread(), ConcurrentHashMap and CopyOnWriteArrayList instead of synchronized wrappers, CountDownLatch and CyclicBarrier for coordination, and CompletableFuture for async pipelines. Know the deadlock ingredients (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait) and how to avoid them: acquire locks in a fixed order, use timeouts (tryLock), and keep critical sections small. Always shut down an ExecutorService, or the JVM will not exit.
question: Module 0 revision: Concurrency in one minute
shortAnswer: Threads share heap memory; synchronize access to shared mutable state, prefer java.util.concurrent utilities over raw wait/notify, and use ExecutorService instead of creating threads by hand.
title: Revision: Concurrency basics

detailedAnswer: Without synchronization, one thread's write to a shared variable may never become visible to another thread, and the JVM or CPU may reorder operations. The Java Memory Model fixes this with happens-before relationships: a write happens-before a later read if they are ordered by a rule such as: unlocking a monitor happens-before locking the same monitor; a write to a volatile variable happens-before a later read of that volatile; starting a thread happens-before its first action; and a thread's last action happens-before another thread's join() on it. Practical consequences: publish shared state safely (final fields, volatile, or proper synchronization), do not rely on Thread.sleep() for visibility, and remember that 64-bit long/double reads and writes are atomic only if the field is volatile. Double-checked locking is correct only with a volatile instance field.
question: Module 0 revision: Java Memory Model in one minute
shortAnswer: The JMM defines when one thread's writes become visible to another. Happens-before rules — volatile, synchronized, thread start/join, final fields — are what guarantee visibility and ordering.
tips: Frame every JMM answer around one phrase: 'happens-before guarantees visibility and ordering; without it, there is no guarantee at all.'
title: Revision: Java Memory Model

detailedAnswer: Objects start in Eden (young generation); survivors move to survivor spaces and, after enough collections, are promoted to the old generation. Minor GC cleans the young generation and is frequent but cheap; major/full GC cleans the old generation and is rarer but costlier. Modern collectors: G1 (the default since Java 9, region-based, balances latency and throughput), ZGC and Shenandoah (very low pause times, good for large heaps). Reachability, not reference counting, decides liveness — even cyclic references are collected if unreachable. Practical points: avoid finalize() (deprecated, unpredictable), do not call System.gc() in production code, watch for memory leaks via static collections or unclosed listeners/caches holding references, and choose a collector by measuring pause time and throughput, not by reputation.
question: Module 0 revision: Garbage collection in one minute
shortAnswer: The GC reclaims unreachable objects. Most objects die young, so the heap is generational: young generation collected often, old generation rarely. Tune the collector to the app's latency or throughput goal.
tips: If asked 'how would you investigate high GC pauses?', answer: GC logs, heap dump analysis, and checking for allocation hotspots — in that order.
title: Revision: Garbage collection

commonMistakes: Forgetting serialVersionUID and then breaking compatibility on a class change.
Serializing fields that should be transient (passwords, caches).
detailedAnswer: Reflection (Class, Method, Field) lets code inspect types, create instances, and call methods whose names are only known at runtime — frameworks like Spring and Jackson rely on it. Costs: slower than direct calls, breaks encapsulation (setAccessible), and defeats compile-time checking, so prefer it in framework code, not business logic. Serialization (java.io.Serializable) writes an object's state to a stream and reads it back; transient fields are skipped, static fields are not serialized, and serialVersionUID controls version compatibility — change the class without updating it and deserialization fails. Security warning: never deserialize untrusted data with native Java serialization; prefer JSON (Jackson) for data exchange. For deep copies, serialization works but is slow — consider a copy constructor or a mapping library instead.
question: Module 0 revision: Reflection and serialization in one minute
shortAnswer: Reflection inspects and invokes classes at runtime; serialization converts an object graph to bytes and back. Both are powerful and both bypass normal compile-time safety — use them deliberately.
title: Revision: Reflection and serialization

detailedAnswer: The flow is: DriverManager (or a DataSource) gives a Connection, you create a Statement or PreparedStatement, execute a query, and read the ResultSet. Always prefer PreparedStatement over Statement: parameters are bound safely, which prevents SQL injection and lets the database reuse execution plans. Close Connection, Statement, and ResultSet in reverse order — try-with-resources does this for you. Handle SQLException (checked) by translating it into a meaningful application exception and rolling back the transaction where needed. In real applications, never open a raw connection per request: use a connection pool such as HikariCP (Spring Boot's default) and let Spring's JdbcTemplate or Spring Data JPA handle the boilerplate. Know the transaction basics: auto-commit off, commit on success, rollback on failure.
question: Module 0 revision: JDBC in one minute
shortAnswer: JDBC is Java's API for relational databases: load a driver, get a Connection, use PreparedStatement for parameterized SQL, close everything with try-with-resources, and pool connections in production.
tips: The one JDBC answer interviewers always want: PreparedStatement prevents SQL injection; Statement with string concatenation does not.
title: Revision: JDBC

detailedAnswer: SOLID: S — a class has one reason to change; O — open for extension, closed for modification (extend via new code, not edits); L — a subclass must be usable wherever its superclass is expected; I — many small interfaces beat one fat interface; D — depend on abstractions, not concretions (this is what Spring DI implements). Patterns to name with an example each: Singleton (one instance — use an enum or Spring's singleton scope, not a hand-rolled double-checked lock unless asked); Factory (create objects without exposing construction logic); Builder (readable construction of objects with many optional fields); Strategy (swap algorithms at runtime, e.g. payment methods); Observer (notify subscribers of state changes); Decorator (add behaviour without subclassing); Adapter (make incompatible interfaces work together); Repository (abstract data access behind an interface). Never recite patterns without an example — one real use case each is what scores.
question: Module 0 revision: Design patterns and SOLID in one minute
shortAnswer: SOLID: single responsibility, open/closed, Liskov substitution, interface segregation, dependency inversion. Patterns to know cold: Singleton, Factory, Builder, Strategy, Observer, Decorator, Adapter, Repository.
tips: When asked for a pattern, name it, state the problem it solves, then give a one-line example from a real codebase.
title: Revision: Design patterns and SOLID

detailedAnswer: Inversion of Control flips responsibility: instead of a class creating its own dependencies with new, the Spring container instantiates beans and injects their dependencies. Dependency injection comes in three forms — constructor injection (preferred: dependencies are final, the object is never half-built, and testing is easy), setter injection, and field injection (avoid: hidden dependencies, hard to test). Stereotype annotations mark beans for component scanning: @Component (general), @Service (business logic), @Repository (data access, also translates persistence exceptions), @Controller/@RestController (web layer). @Bean methods in a @Configuration class define beans explicitly, e.g. third-party classes you cannot annotate. Bean scopes: singleton (default, one per container), prototype (new instance per request), plus request/session scopes in web apps. Lifecycle hooks: @PostConstruct for setup after injection, @PreDestroy for cleanup.
question: Module 0 revision: Spring IoC in one minute
shortAnswer: IoC means the container creates and wires beans instead of your code doing it. Inject via constructor (preferred), declare beans with @Component/@Service/@Repository or @Bean, and let Spring manage their lifecycle.
tips: If asked 'why constructor injection?', the answer is three words: immutability, testability, fail-fast — missing dependencies fail at startup, not at runtime.
title: Revision: Spring IoC and dependency injection

detailedAnswer: @SpringBootApplication is three annotations in one: @Configuration (this class defines beans), @EnableAutoConfiguration (let Boot configure beans for you), and @ComponentScan (find your @Component classes). Auto-configuration classes, listed in Spring Boot's auto-configuration imports, create beans only when conditions hold — @ConditionalOnClass (a library is present), @ConditionalOnMissingBean (you have not defined your own), @ConditionalOnProperty (a property is set). That is why adding spring-boot-starter-web gives you an embedded Tomcat and a DispatcherServlet with no XML, and why defining your own DataSource bean replaces Boot's default. Configuration comes from application.properties or application.yml, bound to type-safe classes with @ConfigurationProperties, and overridden per environment with Spring profiles (@Profile, spring.profiles.active). Debug with --debug or the conditions report to see which auto-configurations matched and why others did not.
question: Module 0 revision: Spring Boot auto-configuration in one minute
shortAnswer: @SpringBootApplication bundles @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, and @ComponentScan. Auto-configuration supplies beans conditionally, based on what is on the classpath and what you have already defined.
tips: The killer interview line: auto-configuration backs off when you define your own bean — @ConditionalOnMissingBean is the mechanism.
title: Revision: Spring Boot auto-configuration

commonMistakes: Using GET with a body or POST for pure reads.
detailedAnswer: The DispatcherServlet is the front controller: it receives every request, consults handler mappings to find the matching @Controller method, resolves arguments (@PathVariable, @RequestParam, @RequestBody), and writes the response via message converters (JSON with Jackson by default). @RestController is @Controller + @ResponseBody — it returns data, not views. REST conventions: GET for reads (200), POST for creation (201 with a Location header), PUT for full replacement, PATCH for partial updates, DELETE for removal (204), and 404 for missing resources, 400 for invalid input, 401/403 for auth problems. Validate request bodies with Bean Validation (@Valid, @NotNull, @Size) and return field errors cleanly. Centralize error handling with @ControllerAdvice + @ExceptionHandler so controllers stay focused on happy paths. Keep controllers thin: they translate HTTP to service calls and back, and all business logic lives in services.
question: Module 0 revision: Spring MVC and REST in one minute
shortAnswer: DispatcherServlet routes requests to @RestController methods. Use @GetMapping/@PostMapping with proper status codes, validate input, and handle errors centrally with @ControllerAdvice.
title: Revision: Spring MVC and REST

detailedAnswer: Define an interface extending JpaRepository<Entity, Id> and Spring Data generates the implementation at runtime: save, findById, findAll, delete, plus derived queries parsed from method names (findByEmailAndActiveTrue). For anything the naming rules cannot express, write @Query with JPQL or a native query. Entities map tables with @Entity, @Id, @GeneratedValue, and relationships @OneToMany/@ManyToOne — fetch type matters: LAZY loads associations on access, EAGER loads them immediately, and lazy access outside a transaction throws LazyInitializationException. The N+1 problem (one query for parents, then one per child) is fixed with JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, or a DTO projection. Transactions belong on service methods with @Transactional (rollback by default only for unchecked exceptions), and read-only transactions (readOnly = true) are a cheap optimization for queries.
question: Module 0 revision: Spring Data JPA in one minute
shortAnswer: Spring Data JPA generates repository implementations from interfaces: derived query methods, @Query for custom JPQL, and @Transactional boundaries on services — with lazy loading and the N+1 problem as the classic traps.
tips: When asked about N+1, name the symptom (many small queries), the cause (lazy loading in a loop), and the fix (JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph) — all three in one breath.
title: Revision: Spring Data JPA in one minute

commonMistakes: Storing secrets or passwords in a JWT payload.
Accepting tokens without verifying signature or expiry.
Storing passwords in plain text or with a fast hash like MD5.
detailedAnswer: Authentication (who are you?) happens first, via login credentials, OAuth2, or a token; authorization (what may you do?) follows, via roles or authorities (ROLE_USER, ROLE_ADMIN). In Spring Security, a filter chain intercepts requests, an AuthenticationManager verifies credentials, and a SecurityContext holds the authenticated principal for the request. A JWT has three Base64URL parts: header (algorithm), payload (claims such as sub, roles, exp), and signature (HMAC or RSA over header + payload). The server verifies the signature with its secret or public key and rejects expired tokens — the payload is readable by anyone, so never put secrets in it. Access tokens are short-lived; refresh tokens (stored securely, ideally httpOnly) issue new ones. Stateless JWT auth scales because no server-side session is needed, but tokens cannot be revoked before expiry without a denylist — keep lifetimes short. Always serve auth over HTTPS, store passwords hashed with BCrypt (never plain or MD5), and protect against CSRF where cookies carry auth.
question: Module 0 revision: Security and JWT in one minute
shortAnswer: Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do. JWT is a signed, stateless token: header.payload.signature — verify the signature and expiry, never trust the payload alone.
title: Revision: Security and JWT

detailedAnswer: A microservice owns one bounded context and its own database — no shared tables across services, or you have a distributed monolith, not microservices. Services communicate synchronously (REST, gRPC) or asynchronously (events via Kafka/RabbitMQ); async messaging decouples services but introduces eventual consistency, so design for it (idempotent consumers, outbox pattern for reliable publishing). Cross-cutting concerns: an API gateway for routing and auth, service discovery for locating instances, centralized configuration, distributed tracing (trace IDs across calls), and resilience patterns — timeouts, retries with backoff, and circuit breakers. Spring Boot Actuator adds production endpoints: /actuator/health (liveness and readiness), /actuator/metrics (JVM, HTTP, custom counters via Micrometer), /actuator/info, and /actuator/env. Expose health publicly if needed, but restrict metrics and env behind authentication — they leak internals. Pair Actuator with Prometheus/Grafana for metrics and a log aggregator for logs.
question: Module 0 revision: Microservices and Actuator in one minute
shortAnswer: Microservices split a system into independently deployable services, each owning its data. Actuator exposes health, metrics, and info endpoints so you can observe them — but expose only what is safe.
tips: If asked 'monolith or microservices?', answer with trade-offs: microservices buy independent scaling and deployment but cost operational complexity — do not present them as always better.
title: Revision: Microservices and Actuator

detailedAnswer: Records (Java 16) are concise immutable data carriers: record Point(int x, int y) {} generates the constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode, and toString — use them for DTOs and value objects, not for mutable entities. Sealed classes (Java 17) restrict which classes may extend them (permits), making hierarchies exhaustive for switch expressions. Pattern matching for instanceof (Java 16) removes casts: if (obj instanceof String s) { use s directly }. Switch expressions (Java 14) return values and support arrow syntax, and pattern matching for switch (Java 21) matches on types and guards. Text blocks (Java 15) write multiline strings with """ without escaping every quote — ideal for SQL and JSON samples. var (Java 10) infers local variable types but is not dynamic typing and cannot be used for fields or method signatures. Virtual threads (Java 21) make blocking-style code scale to millions of threads, but do not fix shared-state bugs — synchronization rules still apply.
question: Module 0 revision: Modern Java features in one minute
shortAnswer: Records for data carriers, sealed classes for closed hierarchies, pattern matching for instanceof and switch, text blocks for multiline strings, and var for local type inference.
tips: Name the Java version for each feature — interviewers use version numbers to check whether knowledge is current.
title: Revision: Modern Java features
